cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may permanently terminate parental rights, and that intermediate standard — rather than proof beyond a reasonable doubt — satisfies due process.
cases.quote: We hold that such a standard adequately conveys to the factfinder the level of subjective certainty about his factual conclusions necessary to satisfy due process.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the federal constitutional floor that Alaska implements through AS 47.10.088 and CINA Rule 18(c), which require clear and convincing evidence of the statutory termination grounds.

cases.case_name: Stanley v. Illinois
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A State may not remove children from a parent's custody without a hearing on that parent's fitness; denying such a hearing to unwed fathers while granting it to all other parents violates due process and equal protection.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.INP-12: Fixes the constitutional rule that protective custody must be followed by a prompt adversarial hearing on parental fitness, which Alaska implements as the AS 47.10.142(d) temporary-custody hearing.
relevance.ACT-05: Confirms that orders restricting a parent's custody or contact require an individualized hearing rather than a categorical presumption of unfitness.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative federal constitutional duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, so a caseworker's failure to remove a child who is later injured by a parent is not itself a § 1983 due-process violation.
cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

relevance.OUT-06: Explains why a child's death or serious injury at a caregiver's hands generally cannot be redressed as a federal due-process claim, pushing families toward Alaska state-law negligence theories.
relevance.FAIL-04: Marks the boundary of federal § 1983 liability for agency inaction, which is why Alaska failure-to-protect suits proceed under state tort law rather than the Fourteenth Amendment.
relevance.FAIL-02: Distinguishes state inaction (no federal duty) from affirmative state seizure of a child, which does trigger Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment scrutiny.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: "Domicile" in ICWA is a uniform question of federal law, and children domiciled on a reservation fall within exclusive tribal jurisdiction that parents cannot defeat by giving birth or placing the child off-reservation.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States.

relevance.INP-11: Establishes that ICWA's jurisdictional terms are federal and uniform, the premise Alaska courts build on when allocating authority between the superior court and Alaska Native tribal courts.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A social worker who removed children without a warrant was denied qualified immunity because no exigency existed; the agency's own decision to treat the report as a non-emergency ten-day response, and its ability to obtain a warrant within hours, defeated any claim of imminent danger.
cases.quote: Here, the concerned officials classified the case as a ten-day response, indicating that they did not think that any exigency existed.

relevance.INP-01: Shows that how the agency itself triages an incoming report is evidence of whether the reported conditions posed imminent danger.
relevance.INP-02: Treats the agency's own screening classification of a third-party report as probative of the absence of emergency.
relevance.INP-06: Confirms that a hotline report the agency grades as non-urgent cannot later be recast as the basis for warrantless emergency action.
relevance.INP-10: Makes the screening-to-investigation classification legally consequential, not merely administrative.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that the availability of a warrant within hours defeats a claim of protective-custody exigency.
relevance.DEC-01: Establishes that a screening decision treating a report as non-urgent is admissible against the agency on the exigency question.
relevance.DEC-02: Ties the response-time decision made at acceptance to the constitutional analysis of any later removal.
relevance.DEC-04: States the controlling Ninth Circuit rule that warrantless removal is permissible only on genuine exigency.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is the circuit's leading case denying qualified immunity to a caseworker for a warrantless removal without exigency.

cases.case_name: Calabretta v. Floyd
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A social worker and police officer were denied qualified immunity for coercing entry into a home and strip-searching a child to investigate an anonymous abuse tip, because a child-abuse investigation is not an exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant, consent, or exigency requirements.
cases.quote: A social worker is not entitled to sacrifice a family's privacy and dignity to her own personal views on how parents ought to discipline their children.

relevance.INP-01: Holds that a report of suspected abuse, standing alone, does not authorize a coerced entry to verify it.
relevance.INP-02: Establishes that an unverified third-party report gives investigators no special dispensation from the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.INP-03: Addresses a joint social-worker/police home visit and holds neither official was immune for the warrantless entry.
relevance.INP-06: Holds that an anonymous tip about screaming, without corroboration, does not create the special exigency needed for entry.
relevance.INP-07: Governs the warrantless physical examination of a child's body during an abuse investigation.
relevance.INP-08: Governs the coercive interview of a child conducted as part of a maltreatment investigation.
relevance.DEC-02: Marks the constitutional limits on what investigators may do once a report is accepted for investigation.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows that a delayed, low-urgency investigation cannot support an exigency claim for entry or seizure.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is foundational Ninth Circuit authority that child-protection investigation is not a Fourth Amendment exception.

cases.case_name: Capp v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A parent stated a viable First Amendment retaliation claim, not defeated by qualified immunity, where he alleged a social worker threatened his custody in retaliation for his criticism of the agency and would not have taken that step absent retaliatory animus.
cases.quote: We also conclude, however, that Plaintiffs plead a viable First Amendment retaliation claim, and that Defendants are not entitled to qualified immunity on this claim.

relevance.DEC-03: Addresses a parent's challenge to a central-index abuse listing and the retaliation theory available when such a finding is animated by improper motive.
relevance.FAIL-05: Is the controlling circuit authority allowing a § 1983 retaliation claim against child-welfare workers who act against a parent for protected speech.

cases.case_name: Rowan B. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Civil discovery rules, not the Public Records Act exemptions, govern a CINA parent's request for law-enforcement records, and the trial court erred by denying the request outright instead of conducting an in camera review.
cases.quote: We hold that the trial court erred in denying Rowan access to materials he sought through discovery without at least conducting an in camera review.

relevance.INP-01: Governs a parent's access to the underlying reports and investigative records generated by a mandated report.
relevance.INP-03: Holds that law-enforcement reports underlying a CINA case are reachable through civil discovery, subject to in camera review.
relevance.INP-08: Applies to school- and agency-generated investigative records a parent seeks to test at adjudication.
relevance.DEC-01: Gives parents a discovery route to the screening and report records that explain why matters were opened or closed.
relevance.DEC-03: Ensures the evidentiary basis of a substantiation is testable through discovery before adjudication.
relevance.DEC-05: Establishes that Alaska Civil Rules 26-37 and 45 apply once a CINA petition is filed.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is a reversal of a trial court's blanket confidentiality ruling, the paradigm procedural-error reversal in a CINA case.
relevance.FAIL-06: Rejects agency reliance on Public Records Act exemptions as a basis for withholding records from a party litigant.
relevance.PMC-05: Distinguishes public-records requests from party discovery, a distinction any transparency effort in Alaska must respect.

cases.case_name: Christopher C. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights to Indian children, holding that failure to remedy and active efforts must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, that best interests is found by a preponderance, and that placement objections — including cultural ones — belong in a placement review, not the termination trial.
cases.quote: Challenges to placement decisions, including challenges based on cultural concerns, are not properly raised in a termination proceeding.

relevance.DEC-03: Sets out the evidentiary showings OCS must ultimately carry after a substantiated finding leads to a termination petition.
relevance.ACT-02: Confirms that the adequacy of court-ordered services is litigated as the reasonable/active efforts element.
relevance.ACT-03: Holds that a parent must contest a foster placement through placement review rather than at the termination trial.
relevance.OUT-02: States Alaska's layered termination standard: clear and convincing evidence on the grounds, preponderance on best interests.

cases.case_name: Anton K. v. State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: ICWA's active-efforts duty continues even while a parent is incarcerated — incarceration affects only what efforts are possible — and the court affirmed termination after finding OCS's efforts, viewed in their entirety, were active.
cases.quote: ICWA also does not contain any provision allowing a court to approve the discontinuation of active efforts.

relevance.INP-12: Requires active efforts to avoid removal of an Indian child even at the emergency-custody stage.
relevance.ACT-02: Holds that the duty to provide remedial services cannot be judicially suspended, however long the case has run.
relevance.OUT-01: Preserves the reunification obligation even when permanency timelines press against it.
relevance.OUT-02: Bars termination of rights to an Indian child unless active efforts are proved by clear and convincing evidence.

cases.case_name: Demetria H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: An ICWA qualified expert witness need not have met the child or family so long as the court has sufficient information about the family's particular circumstances, and the court may aggregate expert and lay testimony to support the serious-harm finding.
cases.quote: The trial court did not err in qualifying Kaufman as an expert witness or using his testimony to support its substantial risk of harm finding.

relevance.INP-11: Defines who may serve as the ICWA qualified expert once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls the qualified-expert-witness element of the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt serious-harm finding required to terminate rights to an Indian child.
relevance.FAIL-05: Shows that the expert's familiarity with the Tribe's prevailing social and cultural standards is a reviewable safeguard against culturally uninformed findings.

cases.case_name: Native Village of Tununak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Overruling its prior application of Adoption Rule 11's preponderance standard, the court held that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, and vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
cases.quote: we conclude that ICWA implicitly mandates that good cause to deviate from ICWA's adoptive placement preferences be proved by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.INP-11: Demonstrates that ICWA supplies a federal standard of proof that displaces a conflicting Alaska court rule.
relevance.ACT-04: Raises the State's burden when it proposes to bypass an extended-family or tribal placement.
relevance.OUT-02: Governs the placement determination that accompanies adoption after termination of parental rights.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is a vacatur of a superior court placement ruling for applying the wrong standard of proof.
relevance.FAIL-03: Illustrates state practice being corrected for falling below a federal statutory requirement.
relevance.FAIL-05: Protects Indian children and tribes against deviations from congressionally mandated placement preferences on a weak evidentiary showing.

cases.case_name: In re Adoption of Sara J.
cases.holding: The prevailing social and cultural standards of the Indian community do not themselves govern the good-cause determination under ICWA § 1915, but remain relevant to the suitability of a preferred placement and may inform a special-needs good-cause finding; the good-cause findings here were affirmed.
cases.quote: They may also inform, but need not control, any determination of whether a child's special needs or other circumstances constitute good cause to deviate from the preferences.

relevance.ACT-04: Defines the role tribal social and cultural standards play when the agency proposes to depart from the kinship and tribal placement preferences.
relevance.OUT-03: Applies to permanency placements achieved through adoption or kin caregiving where ICWA preferences are in play.

cases.case_name: State v. Native Village of Tanana
cases.holding: Federally recognized Alaska Native tribes may exercise inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate ICWA child custody proceedings without a § 1918 reassumption petition, and judgments from those proceedings may be entitled to full faith and credit by the State.
cases.quote: federally recognized Alaska Native tribes are not necessarily precluded from exercising inherent sovereign jurisdiction to initiate "child custody proceedings" as ICWA defines that term

relevance.INP-11: Is the controlling Alaska authority on when a tribal forum, rather than the superior court, may open a child-protection case.
relevance.FAIL-03: Rejected a State policy position (the 2004 Attorney General opinion) that had denied recognition to tribal child-welfare judgments.
relevance.PMC-01: Any Alaska performance review must account for cases resolved in tribal courts whose judgments the State must recognize.
relevance.PMC-06: Shows that an Alaska decision chain is incomplete unless it models concurrent tribal jurisdiction alongside the state pathway.

cases.case_name: Simmonds v. Parks
cases.holding: Adopting the federal tribal-exhaustion doctrine, the court held that a father who failed to appeal a Minto Tribal Court termination of his parental rights through tribal appellate remedies could not collaterally attack that judgment in state court, and his suit was dismissed.
cases.quote: We therefore conclude his suit in Alaska state court must be dismissed.

relevance.INP-11: Establishes that once a tribal court properly exercises jurisdiction, tribal remedies must be exhausted before any state-court challenge.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows that a state-court action will be dismissed outright where tribal remedies were not exhausted.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services v. Michelle P.
cases.holding: CINA jurisdiction derives from the child's status as a child in need of aid and is distinct from a custody or supervision grant, so dismissal of the petition was reversed; separately, the removal order was vacated because it lacked sufficient evidentiary support and did not satisfy ICWA.
cases.quote: This was error because the removal order was not supported by sufficient evidence and did not comply with the requirements of the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA).

relevance.INP-04: Clarifies that the court's CINA jurisdiction continues independent of the disposition order that referred the family for supervision.
relevance.INP-10: Anchors the agency's authority to escalate in the child's adjudicated status rather than in the custody order.
relevance.INP-12: Vacates a removal order for evidentiary insufficiency, the direct check on protective-custody decisions.
relevance.DEC-04: Holds that an order removing a child must rest on sufficient evidence and, for Indian children, on ICWA-compliant findings.
relevance.DEC-05: Reverses a dismissal of a CINA petition and explains what keeps the dependency case open.
relevance.ACT-03: Vacates a foster-care removal order that lacked the required evidentiary and ICWA findings.
relevance.ACT-05: Confirms the court retains authority to enter protective orders in the CINA case so long as jurisdiction persists.
relevance.OUT-05: Holds the superior court erred in dismissing the case for want of jurisdiction.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is a reversal of an erroneous trial-court disposition of an agency petition.
relevance.FAIL-02: Vacates a removal order for insufficient evidence — the state-law analogue to an unlawful-removal claim.

cases.case_name: Reasner v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Summary judgment against a former foster child who sued OCS over years of sexual abuse was vacated because a genuine factual dispute existed about when she discovered OCS's possible role, though her claim did not qualify for the extended limitations period of AS 09.10.065(a).
cases.quote: We conclude that a genuine factual dispute exists concerning when Reasner discovered information suggesting that OCS had played a role in allowing her to be abused.

relevance.INP-09: Shows that agency conduct in approving and supervising a placement is discoverable and reviewable years later through civil litigation.
relevance.ACT-06: Concerns OCS's responsibility for the care and safety of a child it placed and whose adoption it approved.
relevance.OUT-04: Determines when a youth who was abused in care may still sue after leaving OCS custody.
relevance.OUT-06: Is Alaska's leading authority on the timeliness of a serious-harm claim by a child abused while in state care.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the discovery-rule framework for suits alleging agency responsibility for harm to a supervised child.
relevance.PMC-02: Litigation of this kind is often the only public accounting of how an agency approved and monitored a placement.
relevance.PMC-04: Illustrates why serious-injury cases surface long after the fact, a gap fatality-review systems are meant to close.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services v. Mullins
cases.holding: A jury verdict holding OCS responsible for 95% of the damages suffered by two sisters abused by grandparents while in OCS legal custody was set aside as irrational, and OCS was granted a new trial on allocation of fault.
cases.quote: Because the evidence supporting the jury's allocation of fault was so insubstantial as to make the verdict plainly unreasonable, we conclude that OCS is entitled to a new trial.

relevance.OUT-06: Confirms that OCS can be sued in negligence for harm to children in its legal custody, while limiting how much fault a jury may shift from the actual abuser.
relevance.FAIL-04: Is the leading Alaska case on agency negligence for failing to protect children under its supervision and on the limits of that liability.
relevance.PMC-04: Shows that tort litigation, not a fatality-review process, has been the main public airing of OCS supervision failures in Alaska.

cases.case_name: Jacob v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Grandparents were entitled to a declaratory judgment that OCS violated their statutory rights to notice of and participation in their grandchildren's CINA proceedings, but their remaining claims — including the request for systemic injunctive relief — became moot once they intervened.
cases.quote: We hold that all other issues are moot due to the Jacobs' subsequent intervention in their grandchildren's CINA proceedings.

relevance.INP-05: Establishes that relatives who affirmatively seek placement and information have enforceable statutory rights against OCS.
relevance.ACT-04: Confirms grandparents' statutory entitlement to notice and to be heard when placement of their grandchildren is decided.
relevance.OUT-03: Protects relatives pursuing kinship permanency by guaranteeing notice of permanency hearings.
relevance.DEC-06: Shows that even where no relative petition is filed, OCS owes statutory notice duties to grandparents.
relevance.INP-09: Illustrates how an individual suit exposed an alleged systemic OCS failure to give grandparents statutory notice.
relevance.FAIL-06: Declares OCS's failure to provide statutorily required notice unlawful.
relevance.PMC-01: Documents a systemic notice failure of exactly the kind federal performance reviews are meant to detect.
relevance.PMC-03: Shows why an independent review mechanism matters: mootness barred the plaintiffs from obtaining systemic relief.

cases.case_name: Alex H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: An incarcerated parent who participated telephonically in his termination trial was not denied due process when the superior court declined to order his transport, because he showed no way his in-person presence would have reduced the risk of an erroneous result.
cases.quote: The superior court did not violate Alex's right to due process by declining to order his transport.

relevance.DEC-05: Fixes the participation rights an incarcerated parent holds once a dependency case is opened against him.
relevance.OUT-02: Controls whether an incarcerated Alaska parent may insist on physical presence at a termination trial.

cases.case_name: Basey v. State, Department of Public Safety, Division of Alaska State Troopers
cases.holding: The State failed to establish either the AS 40.25.122 litigation exception or the law-enforcement exception to the Alaska Public Records Act, so dismissal of the records requester's suit was error and the case was remanded.
cases.quote: We conclude it was error for the superior court to grant the State's motion to dismiss pursuant to AS 40.25.122.

relevance.FAIL-06: Places the burden on the State to justify each claimed exemption before it may withhold public records.
relevance.PMC-05: Is the leading recent Alaska authority construing the Public Records Act's exceptions narrowly in favor of disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: Defines the legal basis on which state child-welfare data and records can be compelled into public view.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services v. Zander B.
cases.holding: The superior court acted within its discretion in permitting foster parents to intervene for the limited purpose of challenging OCS's decision to move the child, and its stay of that placement transfer was affirmed.
cases.quote: We hold that the court did not abuse its discretion by permitting intervention under the circumstances of this case.

relevance.ACT-03: Establishes that foster parents may obtain judicial review of an OCS decision to transfer a child's placement.
relevance.PMC-03: Shows that in Alaska, caregiver intervention in court — not a citizen panel — is the practical check on placement-change decisions.

cases.case_name: Taryn M. v. State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Denial of an ICWA-preferred relative's request for placement was affirmed because OCS proved by clear and convincing evidence that she was an unsuitable caretaker for a medically fragile child, although the superior court erred in assigning any burden to the relative.
cases.quote: Because OCS demonstrated by clear and convincing evidence that the relative was an unsuitable caretaker, we affirm the superior court.

relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that OCS, not the caregiver, bears the burden when it declines a statutorily preferred placement.
relevance.ACT-04: Sets the clear-and-convincing burden OCS must carry to reject an ICWA-preferred relative caregiver.
relevance.OUT-03: Governs whether a preferred relative can be excluded from becoming the child's permanent caregiver.

cases.case_name: Native Village of Kwinhagak v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: OCS need not follow the civil commitment statutes to hospitalize a child in its custody for psychiatric care, but the Alaska Constitution's due process clause required prompt notice to the CINA parties and a hearing as soon as reasonably possible; a 46-day delay was unconstitutional and the order was reversed.
cases.quote: Due process also required the court to hold a hearing as soon as reasonably possible to determine whether the hospitalization was justified.

relevance.INP-07: Governs what happens when a healthcare encounter results in a child in state custody being admitted for psychiatric care.
relevance.ACT-06: Is Alaska's controlling authority on the process due when the agency authorizes emergency psychiatric hospitalization of a child in its custody.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services v. Z.C.
cases.holding: In a class action on behalf of foster children whose Social Security benefits OCS applied to reimburse itself, the court held the due-process claim was not federally preempted and that OCS must give the notice ordered by the superior court if it continues its self-reimbursing representative-payee practice.
cases.quote: We therefore hold that OCS must provide the notice ordered by the superior court if it wishes to continue implementing its self-reimbursing rep payee scheme.

relevance.INP-09: A class action, rather than any internal audit, was the mechanism that surfaced and corrected this statewide OCS practice.
relevance.OUT-04: Directly governs the federal benefits of youth in and aging out of Alaska foster care, and the notice they are owed.
relevance.FAIL-03: Adjudicates whether federal Social Security rules displace state due-process obligations OCS owes foster children.
relevance.PMC-01: Identifies a statewide practice affecting every foster child's assets that routine performance monitoring had not remedied.
relevance.PMC-02: Concerns OCS's use of children's federal benefits to reimburse its own costs — a core financial-accountability question.
relevance.PMC-03: Demonstrates that in Alaska, class litigation rather than a citizen panel produced systemic corrective relief.
relevance.PMC-06: A structural agency practice was exposed only by aggregating data across many children's cases.

cases.case_name: Blake J. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: A former foster child's suit over abuse by his adoptive mother was time-barred; neither OCS custody until age 19, collateral estoppel from an earlier guardianship competency ruling, nor equitable tolling saved the claim.
cases.quote: collateral estoppel is not available here because the competency standard in a conservatorship and partial guardianship proceeding is different from the standard of competence necessary to file suit

relevance.OUT-04: Fixes the limitations clock for youth who remain in or age out of OCS custody and later sue over harm suffered in care.
relevance.OUT-06: Shows how severe-abuse claims by former foster children fail on timeliness even where the underlying harm is undisputed.
relevance.FAIL-04: Illustrates the procedural barrier that most often defeats accountability suits for harm to supervised children.
relevance.PMC-04: Demonstrates that abuse in state-approved homes may never be adjudicated on the merits, leaving fatality and serious-injury review as the only accounting.

cases.case_name: Mona J. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: The superior court erred in stating that active efforts depend on a parent's willingness to engage, because the active-efforts inquiry focuses primarily on what OCS did, though the court declined to overturn precedent allowing consideration of parental non-cooperation and futility.
cases.quote: the active efforts inquiry depends primarily on OCS's efforts, not the parent's reaction to those efforts

relevance.ACT-01: Keeps the focus on what services the agency actually offered, not on whether the parent accepted voluntary services.
relevance.ACT-02: Prevents a parent's non-participation from substituting for the agency's obligation to provide court-ordered services.
relevance.OUT-01: Preserves the reunification duty as an agency obligation rather than a conditional offer.
relevance.FAIL-05: Guards against findings that penalize a parent's disengagement instead of examining the adequacy of the agency's outreach.

cases.case_name: Ronald H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Termination of a father's rights to his Indian children, adjudicated in need of aid because of his domestic violence and aggressive behavior, was affirmed because the superior court did not err in finding OCS made active efforts.
cases.quote: We conclude that the superior court did not err in finding that active efforts were made and affirm the termination order.

relevance.ACT-01: Reviews the sufficiency of the service referrals offered to a parent before compulsion was sought.
relevance.ACT-02: Applies the active-efforts review to the domestic-violence and behavioral services ordered in the case plan.
relevance.ACT-05: Addresses a CINA case grounded in domestic violence, where protective measures and services run in parallel.
relevance.OUT-01: Measures whether reunification services were adequate before permanency shifted away from the parent.

cases.case_name: Simone H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: The trial court acted within its discretion in refusing to release the child's therapy records to the mother for use at the termination trial, and substantial evidence supported the finding that OCS made reasonable efforts to reunify the family.
cases.quote: We conclude that the trial court acted within its discretion in denying Simone's request for access to Irving's therapy records

relevance.INP-07: Governs parental access to a child's mental-health treatment records generated during agency involvement.
relevance.ACT-01: Reviews the adequacy of the voluntary services and referrals OCS arranged for the mother.
relevance.ACT-02: Applies the reasonable-efforts standard to the court-ordered service package.
relevance.ACT-06: Addresses the confidentiality of psychological treatment a child receives while in agency custody.
relevance.OUT-01: Confirms reasonable efforts to reunify were made before reunification was abandoned.
relevance.FAIL-06: Marks the limit on disclosure: a child's therapy records may be withheld even from a parent facing termination.
relevance.PMC-05: Shows that child treatment records are a recognized confidentiality boundary any transparency effort must respect.

cases.case_name: Dennis O. v. Stephanie O.
cases.holding: Neither due process nor equal protection required appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in a private child custody modification proceeding where the opposing private party had retained an attorney.
cases.quote: We conclude that due process does not mandate court-appointed counsel for all indigent parents in Dennis's situation

relevance.INP-04: Marks the line between private custody litigation, where counsel is not guaranteed, and state-initiated CINA cases, where AS 18.85.100 provides counsel.
relevance.INP-05: Shows that a parent who seeks relief on his own, without state action against him, has no constitutional claim to appointed counsel.
relevance.DEC-06: Confirms that when no state petition is filed, the procedural protections attached to a dependency case do not attach.

cases.case_name: Dapo v. State, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: In a former foster child's suit arising from abuse by his adoptive mother, the statute of repose applies to OCS's apportionment claim and is not unconstitutional as applied; dismissal of the apportionment claim was reversed and the case remanded.
cases.quote: We hold that the statute of repose applies to the apportionment claim and is not unconstitutional as applied.

relevance.OUT-02: Addresses the State's residual exposure for an adoptive placement it arranged after termination of parental rights.
relevance.OUT-06: Concerns liability allocation for serious abuse suffered by a child the agency placed and whose adoption it approved.
relevance.FAIL-04: Defines the repose and apportionment framework governing claims that OCS bears responsibility for harm to a supervised child.
relevance.PMC-02: Shows how financial responsibility for agency-placement failures is ultimately allocated in Alaska.

cases.case_name: Penn P. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: the superior court's reliance on unadmitted drug-treatment records was harmless, and the father failed to overcome the presumption that counsel's decision not to object was tactical, so he did not show ineffective assistance.
cases.quote: We affirm the termination order because relying on the unadmitted drug-treatment records was harmless error and because the father has not shown that he received ineffective assistance of counsel.

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the standard a parent must meet to upset a termination order on evidentiary or ineffective-assistance grounds.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines when a trial-court error in a CINA case is harmless rather than reversible.

cases.case_name: In re Protective Proceedings of Baron W.
cases.holding: ICWA's active-efforts and serious-damage requirements in 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d)-(f) do not apply to a proceeding removing a guardian of an Indian child, and the superior court's removal of the grandmother as guardian, based on the child's best interests, was affirmed.
cases.quote: We affirm the superior court's removal of the grandmother as guardian.

relevance.INP-05: Shows how a relative's voluntary guardianship can itself become the subject of a protective proceeding when the guardian's conduct endangers the child.
relevance.OUT-03: Is Alaska's controlling authority on the standard for terminating a minor's guardianship, including for an Indian child.

cases.case_name: Amy S. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Assuming without deciding that the superior court violated due process by taking judicial notice of contested facts, pleadings, and testimony from the parents' domestic-relations file when adjudicating the child in need of aid, any error was harmless, and the adjudication was affirmed.
cases.quote: taking judicial notice of the existence of ten years of custody disputes is different than taking judicial notice of specific facts, pleadings, and testimony from the custody case

relevance.INP-01: The record showed most of the many prior reports against these parents were unsubstantiated, and prior reports alone do not establish the facts of a new case.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that a history of third-party reports is not itself proof of the conditions alleged.
relevance.INP-04: Addresses AS 47.10.113, which folds custody questions into the CINA case, and limits how the custody file may be used.
relevance.INP-06: Shows that an accumulation of hotline reports, most unsubstantiated, cannot be treated as established fact.
relevance.INP-08: Limits the use of previously generated case material as substantive evidence about a child's current condition.
relevance.INP-10: Distinguishes a report history that justifies opening an investigation from facts proved at adjudication.
relevance.DEC-01: Records that the vast majority of the reports in this family's history were screened out or unsubstantiated.
relevance.DEC-02: Marks the difference between what supports accepting a case and what supports a finding against a parent.
relevance.DEC-03: Holds that unsubstantiated prior reports cannot be converted into findings by judicial notice.
relevance.DEC-05: Governs the evidentiary basis on which a court may adjudicate a child in need of aid after a petition is filed.
relevance.DEC-06: Shows the consequences of a long history of non-court involvement being imported into a later court case.
relevance.FAIL-01: Defines when a due-process defect at adjudication is harmless rather than grounds for reversal.

cases.case_name: Payton S. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
cases.holding: Although the parents did not receive the notice required before the adjudication and disposition hearing, the defect did not affect the outcome and so did not deprive them of due process; the termination was affirmed on the evidence.
cases.quote: CINA Rule 15(b) requires that parents and other interested parties in an ICWA proceeding receive notice of an adjudication hearing "at least ten days before the hearing"

relevance.DEC-05: States the notice parents and tribes are owed once a CINA petition proceeds to adjudication and disposition.

cases.case_name: John v. Baker
cases.holding: Alaska Native tribes possess inherent, non-territorial sovereign authority to adjudicate child custody disputes between their own members in tribal court, so the superior court erred in refusing to give the Northway Tribal Court judgment effect; the case was remanded to decide whether that judgment should be recognized under comity.
cases.quote: we conclude that Native tribes do possess the inherent sovereign power to adjudicate child custody disputes between tribal members in their own courts

relevance.INP-11: Is the foundational Alaska holding that tribal adjudicatory authority over children does not depend on Indian country, the premise on which Tanana and every later Alaska tribal-jurisdiction case rests.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes that an accurate Alaska decision chain must model a tribal-court pathway existing independently of reservation land and of any ICWA section 1918 reassumption petition.

cases.case_name: Flores v. Flores
cases.holding: The due process clause of the Alaska Constitution entitles an indigent parent to court-appointed counsel in a child custody proceeding in which the opposing parent is represented by counsel supplied by a public agency; because the Children's Rules do not reach divorce cases, counsel must be appointed from the private bar.
cases.quote: This disadvantage is constitutionally impermissible where the other parent has an attorney supplied by a public agency.

relevance.INP-04: Is the Alaska baseline right-to-counsel holding against which any referral into a state-initiated child proceeding must be measured, and the source of the language AS 18.85.100 carries for CINA cases.
relevance.INP-05: Establishes that the constitutional trigger for appointed counsel is the imbalance created by publicly supplied counsel on the other side, not the parent's own decision to seek help.
relevance.DEC-06: Is the precedent Dennis O. declined to extend, marking the outer limit of the right to counsel when no state petition and no state-funded opponent is present.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: Due process does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every parental termination proceeding; the trial court decides case by case under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake, and the refusal to appoint counsel here was not error.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-02: Is the federal companion to Santosky on termination procedure: it sets the constitutional floor for appointed counsel, which Alaska exceeds by statute, so an Alaska practitioner must cite both.
relevance.DEC-05: Fixes the federal minimum for representation once the State petitions to sever the parent-child relationship, the standard against which Alaska's statutory appointment scheme is measured.

cases.case_name: Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Summary judgment for the city was reversed: a jury could find the officers lacked reasonable cause to seize the children without a court order, and, absent a risk that physical evidence would dissipate or an urgent medical problem requiring immediate attention, the state must notify parents and obtain judicial approval before subjecting a seized child to an investigatory physical examination.
cases.quote: the state is required to notify parents and to obtain judicial approval before children are subjected to investigatory physical examinations

relevance.INP-07: Is the controlling Ninth Circuit authority on investigatory medical examination of a child taken into protective custody, requiring parental notice and judicial approval absent dissipating evidence or an urgent medical need.
relevance.INP-12: Holds that a warrantless protective seizure requires specific, articulable evidence of imminent danger and that its scope must be strictly circumscribed by the exigency that justified it.
relevance.DEC-04: Supplies the reasonable-cause and scope limits on an emergency removal decision made without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-06: Distinguishes genuine emergency medical care, which the state may authorize, from investigatory examinations, which it may not conduct without parental notice and a judicial order.
relevance.FAIL-02: Is, with Rogers and Calabretta, the core Ninth Circuit line establishing section 1983 liability for removal and examination of a child without exigency or judicial authorization.

cases.case_name: Camreta v. Greene
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court may review a constitutional ruling at the behest of a government official who prevailed below on qualified immunity, but this case became moot because the child had grown up and moved away, so the Court did not reach the Fourth Amendment question and vacated the Ninth Circuit's in-school seizure holding.
cases.quote: we vacate the part of the Ninth Circuit’s opinion that decided the Fourth Amendment issue

relevance.INP-08: Is the reason no binding Ninth Circuit rule governs the in-school seizure and interview of a suspected child-abuse victim: the holding a practitioner would expect to cite was vacated as moot.
relevance.INP-03: Concerns a joint caseworker-and-deputy interview of a child and leaves the constitutional standard for that joint practice unsettled in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every constitutional challenge to ICWA: Congress had Article I power to enact it, its placement and remedial-effort commands do not unconstitutionally commandeer state legislatures, courts or executive officers, and the equal-protection and nondelegation claims failed for want of standing.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: Settles that ICWA validly binds Alaska's superior courts and OCS, removing the constitutional cloud the Fifth Circuit had cast over 25 U.S.C. section 1912(d).
relevance.ACT-04: Confirms that the section 1915 placement preferences remain enforceable against state agencies, so Tununak, Sara J. and Taryn M. rest on a valid federal command.
relevance.FAIL-03: Supersedes Brackeen v. Haaland, 994 F.3d 249 (5th Cir. 2021), which a footnote in Ronald H. cites as having declared section 1912(d) unconstitutional; counsel must cite the Supreme Court's disposition instead.

cases.case_name: Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody, section 1912(d) requires remedial efforts only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, and section 1915(a) does not bar a non-Indian adoption when no other eligible candidate has sought to adopt; the South Carolina judgment was reversed.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family’s “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent’s rights

relevance.ACT-02: Qualifies the active-efforts propositions Alaska draws from Anton K. and Mona J. by limiting section 1912(d) to cases where termination would break up an existing Indian family.
relevance.ACT-04: Limits the section 1915(a) preferences that Tununak and Sara J. enforce: they do not bar a non-preferred placement when no eligible preferred candidate has come forward.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Health & Social Services, Division of Family & Youth Services v. Native Village of Curyung
cases.holding: Alaska Native villages may sue the Division's director in his official capacity under section 1983 as parens patriae on behalf of their member children to enforce rights created by the Adoption Assistance Act and ICWA — including the right to a case plan — but may not use section 1983 to enforce rights they hold as sovereigns and may not sue the State directly.
cases.quote: the villages may bring suit as parens patriae under § 1983 to enforce rights that are created by the Adoption Assistance Act and the Indian Child Welfare Act

relevance.INP-09: Is the Alaska vehicle by which alleged systemic OCS failures — rather than one family's case — can be brought before a court.
relevance.FAIL-03: Is Alaska's leading authority on private enforcement of federal child-welfare statutes against the State, the closest thing in this jurisdiction to a federal-compliance remedy.
relevance.PMC-01: Shows that alleged statewide failures to meet federal Title IV-E and ICWA requirements reach a court through tribal section 1983 litigation rather than through CFSR monitoring.
relevance.PMC-03: Demonstrates that in Alaska the independent-review function is performed by tribes suing as parens patriae, not by a citizen review panel.
relevance.PMC-06: Confirms that systemic patterns across many children's cases are legally cognizable in Alaska when aggregated by a tribal plaintiff.

cases.case_name: State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services v. Karlie T.
cases.holding: The superior court's dismissal of an emergency CINA petition was reversed in part: the inquiry at that stage is only whether probable cause exists to believe the child is in need of aid, and the domestic-violence evidence sufficed under AS 47.10.011(6) and (8)(B)(i), though (8)(B)(ii) requires that the child actually have been exposed to domestic violence.
cases.quote: we reiterate that the superior court was tasked with making a probable cause determination, not a finding whether the child actually was in need of aid

relevance.INP-12: Is Alaska's controlling recent decision on the AS 47.10.142 emergency-custody pathway and the showing OCS must make to keep a newborn in temporary custody.
relevance.DEC-04: Fixes the standard governing judicial review of an emergency removal: probable cause, not proof that the child is in need of aid.
relevance.ACT-05: Holds that evidence of domestic violence between the parents supports CINA jurisdiction only on the terms each subsection of AS 47.10.011(8)(B) specifies.
relevance.OUT-05: Is the leading Alaska case on when dismissal of a CINA petition at the probable-cause stage is error.
relevance.FAIL-01: Reverses a superior court's dismissal of an agency petition for demanding more than probable cause at the first hearing.

cases.case_name: Office of Public Advocacy v. Superior Court, Third Judicial District
cases.holding: A putative father's parentage may be established in a CINA proceeding on legally sufficient non-genetic evidence, so CINA Rule 2(k)'s definition of "parent" — and the party status and appointed counsel that follow — reaches a person the superior court determines to be a parent without scientific testing.
cases.quote: We conclude that a judicial determination of paternity does not necessarily need underlying scientific, genetic testing in this context

relevance.DEC-05: Determines who becomes a party entitled to counsel and notice once OCS files a CINA petition, the threshold question for every downstream procedural right.
relevance.INP-05: Governs a man who comes forward on his own to claim a child in an open CINA case and seeks recognition as a parent.
relevance.INP-04: Shows how parentage questions that would otherwise belong to a separate action are resolved inside the CINA proceeding itself.

notes: Structural point a lawyer must know: Alaska's Court of Appeals (court_id alaskactapp) has jurisdiction only over criminal, delinquency, extradition, probation/parole and habeas matters. There is no intermediate appellate court for CINA, termination, adoption or guardianship cases — every child-welfare appeal goes directly to the Supreme Court of Alaska. Accordingly every state case in this brief is from the Alaska Supreme Court (court_id 'alaska'), and there are no published intermediate appellate decisions to cite on any of these 42 nodes.

Every case listed was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session (search, then the opinion text endpoint) and each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing whitespace, curly quotes and star-page markers. Every quote was also confirmed to fall inside the majority/lead opinion by locating the opinion-boundary markers in the text (e.g. Santosky's majority runs to the start of Justice Rehnquist's dissent; the Sara J. quote is from Justice Eastaugh's opinion, not Chief Justice Bryner's partial concurrence; the Kirkpatrick quote is from the en banc majority).

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. The 13 'key_cases' already present in the AK node files are all 2022-2025 Alaska Supreme Court memorandum decisions carrying synthetic 'Alaska Supreme Court Case s-#####' citations (e.g. 'Alana M. (Mother) v. State', 'Kash B. (Father) v. State'). None of them is precedential under Alaska Appellate Rule 214, none was retrievable as an on-point published opinion, and none is carried forward here.

Gap — mandatory reporting and reporter immunity (INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-07, INP-08): repeated CourtListener searches of the Alaska Supreme Court and Court of Appeals found no published Alaska appellate decision construing AS 47.17.020 (mandated reporter list), AS 47.17.030 (report contents), AS 47.17.050 (good-faith immunity) or AS 47.17.068 (failure to report). These nodes are therefore mapped to the closest controlling authority on what a report may and may not be used to justify — Calabretta v. Floyd (an uncorroborated tip does not authorize entry or a body search), Rogers v. County of San Joaquin (the agency's own triage of a report bears on exigency), Amy S. (unsubstantiated prior reports are not facts) and Rowan B. (a parent's discovery access to the report record). Practitioners should treat AS 47.17 immunity in Alaska as governed by the statute's text, unconstrued by the state's highest court.

Gap — substantiated findings and a central registry (DEC-03): Alaska has no published Supreme Court decision recognizing a due-process 'name-clearing' hearing right for a person listed on a child-protection registry. The node is served by Capp v. County of San Diego (Ninth Circuit; challenge to a Child Abuse Central Index listing, allowed to proceed as a First Amendment retaliation claim), Amy S. (unsubstantiated reports cannot be judicially noticed as facts) and the downstream burden cases. Counsel should not assume a state-law administrative appeal right exists absent regulation.

Gap — differential/alternative response (DEC-06) and voluntary self-referral (INP-05): no Alaska published appellate opinion construes a formal differential-response track. These nodes are mapped to the nearest authority on what protections do and do not attach when no state petition is filed (Dennis O.) and on the statutory rights relatives hold outside a contested case (Jacob, Baron W.).

Gap — the PMC oversight family (PMC-01 through PMC-06) and FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure): no Alaska or Ninth Circuit decision adjudicates CFSR performance, CAPTA citizen review panels, or the Protect Our Kids Act, and the CFSR framework is not privately enforceable. These nodes are mapped to the Alaska cases that actually performed the accountability function in practice — the Z.C. class action over OCS's self-reimbursing use of foster children's Social Security benefits, Jacob (declaratory judgment that OCS systemically failed to give grandparents statutory notice), Basey (Public Records Act exemptions construed narrowly against the State), Rowan B. and Simone H. (the disclosure/confidentiality boundary), and Reasner, Mullins, Dapo and Blake J. (tort litigation as the de facto serious-injury review mechanism). The dataset should say plainly that Alaska's oversight nodes rest on litigation, not on a statutory review body.

Gap — missing children from care: no Alaska appellate decision was found addressing children who run from or go missing from foster placements. No case is offered for that topic; it is not one of the 42 nodes but was on the research list.

DeShaney is included deliberately as the limiting federal authority for OUT-06, FAIL-04 and FAIL-02: it forecloses the intuitive federal claim that an agency's failure to remove a child violates due process, which is why Alaska failure-to-protect claims (Reasner, Mullins, Dapo, Blake J.) are litigated as state-law negligence and repeatedly founder on limitations, repose and fault-allocation rather than on the merits.

ICWA is the single most consequential doctrine in Alaska child welfare and is deliberately over-represented: Tanana (inherent tribal jurisdiction to initiate ICWA proceedings without a § 1918 reassumption petition), Simmonds v. Parks (tribal exhaustion), Tununak (clear and convincing evidence required to deviate from adoptive placement preferences, overruling prior Adoption Rule 11 practice), Sara J. (role of prevailing tribal social and cultural standards), Demetria H. (qualified expert witness), Taryn M. (OCS bears the clear-and-convincing burden to reject a preferred relative), Anton K./Mona J./Ronald H. (active efforts), and Baron W. (§ 1912(d)-(f) do not reach guardianship-removal proceedings). Holyfield supplies the federal baseline but has limited direct force in Alaska, which has essentially no reservation land — Tanana, not Holyfield, is the operative Alaska rule.

Blythe P. (2023) expressly overrules Zander B. (2020) to the extent Zander B. applied abuse-of-discretion review to an AS 47.10.080(s) placement-transfer decision. Both are listed because Zander B. remains good law on foster-parent intervention, but any placement-transfer brief must lead with Blythe P.

Citations are given in Bluebook form without case names, from the reporter citations carried on the CourtListener cluster. Z.C. has no reporter citation yet in CourtListener and is given in slip form using the Supreme Court docket numbers shown on the opinion's face (S-18249/18259, Opinion No. 7760, March 28, 2025); it is a published opinion, not a memorandum decision. URLs are CourtListener cluster pages; CourtListener canonicalizes the slug on request, so a slug variant will redirect to the correct opinion.

Two quotes are complete clauses rather than complete sentences, used because the full sentence exceeded the 30-word limit and truncating differently would have dropped a qualification: Mona J. ('the active efforts inquiry depends primarily on OCS's efforts, not the parent's reaction to those efforts') and Blake J. ('collateral estoppel is not available here because...'). Both were verified as exact substrings and both carry the operative qualification intact.

Budget discipline: approximately 80 CourtListener API requests were made for this jurisdiction (36 searches, ~44 opinion and cluster retrievals), paced at roughly one request every 2.2 seconds, well inside the 150-request ceiling. No HTTP 429 responses were received.

Missing (for a later pass): John v. Baker, 982 P.2d 738 (Alaska 1999) — the foundational Alaska holding that Alaska Native tribes possess inherent (non-territorial) sovereign jurisdiction over child custody matters. Tanana is expressly framed as revisiting 'the inherent sovereign jurisdiction of Alaska Native tribes recognized over a decade ago in John v. Baker,' and Sara J. cites it. INP-11 is incomplete without it. Citation verified from the text of the fetched Sara J. opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Flores v. Flores, 598 P.2d 893 (Alaska 1979) — the Alaska baseline right to appointed counsel for an indigent parent opposed by state-funded counsel; it is the precedent Dennis O. declines to extend and the source of the OPA statute's language. Required for INP-04/INP-05/DEC-05/DEC-06, where the brief currently relies on Dennis O. alone. Citation verified from the text of the fetched Dennis O. opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the federal due-process standard for appointed counsel in termination proceedings and the direct companion to Santosky. A termination node (OUT-02) and a petition/participation node (DEC-05) that cite Santosky but not Lassiter are half-briefed. Citation verified from the text of the fetched Santosky opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Wallis v. Spencer, 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir. 2000) — the controlling Ninth Circuit authority on warrantless removal plus medical examination and interviewing of a seized child without parental notice or consent. It is the natural authority for INP-07 (medical disclosure) and INP-08 (interviews), both of which the brief currently fills with off-point substitutes, and it strengthens FAIL-02. Citation verified from the text of fetched Ninth Circuit opinions.

Missing (for a later pass): Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011), and the underlying Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009) — the in-school seizure and interview of a suspected child-abuse victim by a caseworker and deputy. INP-08 (educational disclosure) has no case involving a school at all; this is the line of authority a practitioner would expect, including the fact that the Supreme Court vacated the Ninth Circuit's Fourth Amendment holding as moot. Camreta citation verified from the text of a fetched opinion.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — the Supreme Court's rejection of the Article I, anticommandeering, and (for want of standing) equal-protection challenges to ICWA. This brief is deliberately ICWA-heavy and one of its own cases (Ronald H.) carries a footnote citing the now-superseded Fifth Circuit decision, Brackeen v. Haaland, 994 F.3d 249 (5th Cir. 2021), as having 'declared unconstitutional' 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d). Leaving the Supreme Court's disposition out is a live risk of citing overruled authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) — the Supreme Court's construction of the reach of 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) and (f) and of the § 1915(a) placement preferences. It qualifies the active-efforts and placement-preference propositions the brief draws from Anton K., Mona J., Tununak and Sara J. across ACT-02, ACT-04, OUT-02 and INP-11.

Missing (for a later pass): State, Department of Health & Social Services v. Native Village of Curyung, 151 P.3d 388 (Alaska 2006) — Alaska's authority on tribal standing and participation in CINA proceedings, and a companion to Tanana on the State's posture toward tribal child-welfare authority. INP-11 and FAIL-03 both lean on Tanana alone. Citation verified from the text of a fetched Alaska opinion.

CLOSING PASS (2026-09-20): every one of the eight authorities the verifier named as missing was searched for by name and citation on CourtListener, retrieved as a cluster and as opinion text, and read in this session. All eight were real and on point; all eight are now case entries. Each new quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing whitespace, curly quotes and star-page markers, and each was confirmed to sit inside the majority or lead opinion by locating the opinion-boundary markers (John v. Baker's majority by Justice Fabe ends where Chief Justice Matthews's dissent begins; Lassiter's majority by Justice Stewart ends at Chief Justice Burger's concurrence; Brackeen's majority by Justice Barrett ends at the Gorsuch concurrence; Adoptive Couple's majority by Justice Alito ends at Justice Thomas's concurrence; Camreta's majority by Justice Kagan ends at Justice Scalia's concurrence; Wallis, Greene v. Camreta, Curyung, Karlie T. and Office of Public Advocacy are single-opinion decisions with no separate writing).

Added John v. Baker, 982 P.2d 738 (Alaska 1999) for INP-11 and PMC-06: it is the foundational Alaska holding that Alaska Native tribes hold inherent, non-territorial sovereign authority to adjudicate child custody disputes between their members, the premise Tanana later extends to ICWA child custody proceedings. Without it INP-11 rested on Tanana and Simmonds without their source. Note for counsel: John v. Baker also holds that ICWA does not apply to an inter-parental custody dispute, and it remands for a comity analysis rather than compelling recognition of the tribal judgment.

Added Flores v. Flores, 598 P.2d 893 (Alaska 1979) for INP-04, INP-05 and DEC-06: it is the Alaska Constitution's baseline right to appointed counsel for an indigent parent whose opponent has publicly supplied counsel, the precedent Dennis O. declined to extend, and it is also the decision holding that the Children's Rules (and hence the public defender's Title 47 duty) do not reach private divorce-custody litigation. It was not mapped to DEC-05, which already carries six authorities.

Added Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) for OUT-02 and DEC-05: it is the federal due-process companion to Santosky, holding that counsel is not constitutionally required in every termination case and that the question is decided case by case against a presumption tied to physical liberty. A termination brief citing Santosky alone understates how much of Alaska's protection is statutory (AS 18.85.100) rather than federal. CourtListener's cluster carries date_filed 1981-08-28 (the rehearing-denial date); the retrieved opinion text states 'Decided June 1, 1981', which is the date recorded here.

Added Wallis ex rel. Wallis v. Spencer, 202 F.3d 1126 (9th Cir.) for INP-07, INP-12, DEC-04, ACT-06 and FAIL-02: it is the controlling circuit authority requiring parental notice and judicial approval before an investigatory physical examination of a seized child, and it states the imminent-danger and scope limits on warrantless removal. Caveat recorded for accuracy: CourtListener's cluster for the amended opinion (the one published at 202 F.3d 1126) carries date_filed 1999-09-14, the date of the original opinion at 193 F.3d 1054; the amended opinion is conventionally cited as (9th Cir. 2000), and date_decided here is the date CourtListener supplied rather than a date appearing in the opinion text.

Quote caveat for Wallis: the court's sentence opens 'Barring a reasonable concern that material physical evidence might dissipate, [citation], or that some urgent medical problem exists requiring immediate attention, the state is required to notify parents...'. Because a full case citation sits inside that sentence, no contiguous 30-word substring carries both exceptions; the quote used is the operative command and both exceptions are stated in the holding field instead.

Added Camreta v. Greene, 563 U.S. 692 (2011) for INP-08 and INP-03, and Greene v. Camreta, 588 F.3d 1011 (9th Cir. 2009) for INP-08, INP-07, INP-03 and FAIL-02. Read them together and note the vacatur: the Supreme Court held it may review a constitutional ruling at a prevailing immunized official's behest but found the case moot and vacated the part of the Ninth Circuit's opinion deciding the Fourth Amendment issue. The Ninth Circuit's in-school seizure holding is therefore NOT citable as binding law; what survives is its separate holding that excluding a mother from her daughters' sexual-abuse medical examinations violated clearly established Fourteenth Amendment familial rights, which is the quote used here. INP-08 accordingly still has no binding circuit rule on school interviews, only Calabretta's general principle that child-abuse investigation is no Fourth Amendment exception.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) for INP-11, ACT-04 and FAIL-03: it forecloses the Article I and anticommandeering attacks on ICWA and disposes of the equal-protection and nondelegation claims for lack of standing. This directly cures the risk flagged earlier in these notes that Ronald H.'s footnote cites the superseded Fifth Circuit decision, Brackeen v. Haaland, 994 F.3d 249 (5th Cir. 2021), as having declared 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) unconstitutional. It was not mapped to OUT-02, which is already at capacity.

Added Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl, 570 U.S. 637 (2013) for ACT-02 and ACT-04: it limits § 1912(d) to cases where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, holds § 1912(f) inapplicable where the parent never had custody, and holds § 1915(a) no bar where no other eligible preferred candidate has sought to adopt. Any Alaska brief relying on Anton K., Mona J., Tununak or Sara J. must account for these limits. It was not mapped to INP-11 or OUT-02, both of which are at or over capacity.

Added State, Department of Health & Social Services, Division of Family & Youth Services v. Native Village of Curyung, 151 P.3d 388 (Alaska 2006) for INP-09, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-03 and PMC-06: Alaska Native villages may sue OCS's director under § 1983 as parens patriae to enforce Adoption Assistance Act and ICWA rights (including the right to a case plan), but may not enforce their own sovereign rights that way or sue the State directly. This is the closest thing Alaska has to a private federal-compliance remedy and it materially strengthens the PMC oversight family, which previously rested entirely on Z.C., Jacob, Basey and the tort cases.

Added State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services v. Karlie T., 538 P.3d 723 (Alaska 2023) for INP-12, DEC-04, ACT-05, OUT-05 and FAIL-01. This closes the thinnest node in the brief: OUT-05 (case dismissal) previously had one mapped case. Karlie T. is the leading recent Alaska decision on the AS 47.10.142 emergency-custody pathway, holds that the first hearing decides probable cause and not whether the child actually is in need of aid, and construes AS 47.10.011(8)(B)(ii) to require that the child actually have been exposed to domestic violence.

Added Office of Public Advocacy v. Superior Court, Third Judicial District, 462 P.3d 1000 (Alaska 2020) for DEC-05, INP-05 and INP-04: a putative father's parentage may be established in a CINA case on legally sufficient non-genetic evidence, so CINA Rule 2(k)'s definition of 'parent' — and with it party status, notice and appointed counsel — reaches a person the superior court finds to be a parent without scientific testing. This is the threshold question for every procedural right downstream of a filed petition.

Node_map maintenance: the node_map was extended, never reduced. Nine nodes that previously carried a single case (INP-04, INP-05, INP-07, INP-08, INP-10, DEC-01, DEC-06, OUT-05, FAIL-05) now carry two or more. Where a node still fell short after the new authorities were mapped, it was filled from existing case entries whose own relevance text already named that node but which the node_map had omitted — an internal-consistency repair, not a new legal claim. All 42 nodes now carry between two and six cases, with the single exception noted next.

OUT-02 carries seven cases rather than the usual maximum of six. The existing six (Santosky, Christopher C., Demetria H., Tununak, Penn P., Alex H.) were left in place because each states a distinct element of Alaska termination practice, and Lassiter was added because the verifier correctly identified a termination node citing Santosky without its federal companion on counsel as half-briefed. No existing mapping was deleted to make room.
